stories.title: Brand Urban Hires Team of Six From Alvarez & Marsal to Expand Retail Services
stories.excerpt: Retail advisory firm Brand Urban is expanding its headcount with the addition of a team from another New York City brokerage, Commercial Observer has learned. Founded by Taryn Brandes, Brand Urban is bringing on Matthew Krell, Daniel Bodner and Lucas Kooyman as well as three others from Alvarez & Marsal Property Solutions in an effort to broaden the range and scale of its services, according to the two firms. Krell will join Brand Urban as principal, while Bodner and Kooyman join as executive vice president and vice president, respectively. The three other new hires from Alvarez & Marsal include Max Swerdloff, Rikard Cederberg and Isabel Krajovan. The hiring of the Alvarez & Marsal team members brings with them clients such as Asana Partners, Nuveen Real Estate and Kushner Companies, as well as retailers such as Patagonia, Lush, Ghirardelli and Barcelona Wine Bar. “At Brand Urban, we’ve been incredibly thoughtful — some would say slow, I would say thoughtful — about growing the team,” Brandes told CO. “We’ve been thoughtful about leadership, we’ve been thoughtful about the individuals we bring into the firm and the clients that we partner with. The addition of Matt and his team is about strengthening our leadership given his experience on the operation and management side of brokerage.” Brandes has built the business from a New York City brokerage into a larger national framework through partnerships helping retailers expand nationally. Customers have included delivery-oriented eatery Goop Kitchen, cafe chain Maman and grocery chain Trader Joe’s. “Gut instincts still matter in this business, but our clients expect recommendations backed by real market intelligence, and Brand Urban has consistently expanded in its service offerings and invested in the data and research capabilities,” Krell said. “The additional services of place-making and growth advisory services were really attractive to our team. stories.impact: Minimal impact on multifamily development; this is a retail brokerage consolidation and does not affect apartment supply, demand, capital, or cost.

stories.title: For Data Centers, the Case for a Local Balance Sheet
stories.excerpt: Every data center project generates an enormous amount of information: engineering reports, environmental filings, utility dockets, tax incentive applications, economic impact studies and public statements. What it rarely generates is a single place where all of that information comes together. A recent dispute in Fayette County, Ga, illustrates why that matters. Questions over water use, utility billing and public communication produced multiple explanations from different parties, each accurate within its own context but difficult for residents, regulators and policymakers to reconcile. The episode was less about assigning blame than about exposing a broader problem: Data center projects are evaluated through documents that were never designed to fit together. Suhail Y Tayeb. PHOTO: Courtesy NYU That is becoming a challenge because the people evaluating these projects are not all asking the same questions or working from the same information. Developers, investors, utilities, regulators and communities often see only the portion of a project that falls within their own responsibility. Over the last several months, I have written about jobs, electricity costs, water and transparency. Those were never separate issues. They are different symptoms of the same underlying problem. The information needed to evaluate a project exists, but it is fragmented across agencies, reports and stages of development. The industry does not need standardized development. Different workloads require different infrastructure. A hyperscale artificial intelligence training campus, an enterprise co-location facility, an edge location serving latency-sensitive applications, and a disaster recovery site solve different problems and therefore require different designs. Those differences are shaped by local power systems, water availability, fiber connectivity and community priorities. Trying to standardize projects would make little sense. bullets: Data center disputes in Fayette County, Ga highlight fragmented project evaluation
Different stakeholders see only portion of project within their responsibility
Infrastructure conflicts over water use, utility billing, public communication unresolved
stories.summary: A recent dispute at a data center project in Fayette County, Georgia exposed a structural problem: data center developments are evaluated through siloed documents (engineering reports, environmental filings, utility dockets, tax applications) that don't align, leaving residents, regulators, and policymakers unable to reconcile conflicting information. The issue is less about blame than process—stakeholders including developers, investors, utilities, and communities each see only their portion of the project.
stories.impact: Indirect relevance to multifamily: data center competition for land, utilities, and capital in growth markets (especially tech hubs like Atlanta submarkets) can constrain multifamily site availability and raise infrastructure costs. Regulatory fragmentation around data centers may tighten entitlements broadly, slowing multifamily development timelines in affected metros.

stories.title: Data Center Giant Equinix Ups Its 2026 Forecast Behind Robust Q2
stories.excerpt: Equinix significantly increased its forecasts and expectations for 2026 after posting another record-heavy quarter on the back of artificial intelligence demand and more data center construction. The Redwood City, Calif.-based data center real estate investment trust (REIT) generated $2.63 billion in second-quarter revenue, up 7 percent from $2.44 billion in the first quarter and 16 percent from $2.26 billion a year earlier. Equinix said operating growth and one-time fees from the company’s xScale hyperscale business boosted its results. Net income reached $477 million, up from $415 million in the first quarter and $367 million during the second quarter of 2025. Net income attributable to common shareholders totaled $479 million, or $4.83 per share. Funds from operations (FFO), REITs’ main cash flow measure, rose to $854 million from $758 million in the previous quarter and $689 million a year earlier. Equinix delivered $424 million in annualized gross bookings, its highest second-quarter total and second-highest quarterly volume on record. Bookings increased from $378 million during the first quarter and $345 million in the second quarter of 2025. The company also generated approximately $110 million in pre-sales. “The vast majority of our largest deals were driven by AI workloads,” CEO Adaire Fox-Martin said Wednesday during the company’s earnings call. She added that Equinix’s revised outlook “reflects a market opportunity that has materially improved over the past 12 months.” Stabilized data centers remained approximately 82 percent utilized, in line with the first quarter. The stabilized portfolio generated $1.89 billion in revenue, up 7 percent annually, while producing a 27 percent cash return on gross property investment, compared with 24 percent a year earlier. bullets: Equinix Q2 2026 revenue $2.63B (+16% YoY); FFO $854M (+24% QoQ)

stories.summary: Equinix reported record Q2 revenue of $2.63 billion (up 16% YoY) and net income of $477 million, driven by artificial intelligence demand and strong xScale hyperscale business performance. FFO grew to $854 million, and annualized gross bookings reached $424 million, its second-highest quarterly total. The Redwood City-based data center REIT significantly increased its 2026 forecast based on sustained momentum.
stories.impact: Strong data center REIT performance signals robust capital availability and investor appetite for infrastructure. This capital inflow into data centers—especially in major tech metros (Bay Area, Austin, Northern Virginia, Phoenix)—competes for development land, equity, and debt. Multifamily developers in these markets face tighter land availability, higher acquisition costs, and potential capital displacement as data center projects accelerate.

stories.title: U.S. Apartment Rents Post Eighth Consecutive Month of Growth
stories.excerpt: U.S. apartment rents were essentially flat in July, with the national average rising +0.03% to $1,747 from June’s upwardly revised level of $1,746, CoStar Group’s Apartments.com reported Wednesday. This marks the eighth consecutive month of positive rent increases following a period of flat to declining monthly performance in the second half of 2025. On an annual basis, rent growth accelerated to +1.0% in July 2026 from the upwardly revised +0.9% in June and was slightly down from the +1.1% reading recorded one year earlier. June 2026 was initially reported as a +0.1% month-over-month increase and has been revised upward to +0.2%. Although apartment rent growth typically slows as the market moves further into the summer leasing season, gains in July were particularly subdued. “Following modest rent increases during the spring, the +0.03% increase recorded in July represents a notable slowdown in monthly pricing momentum,” according to Apartments.com. “While annual rent growth continues to improve gradually, elevated supply levels continue to restrain pricing momentum nationally.” Where the apartment industry connects. Build relationships, uncover opportunities, and stay ahead of what’s next. The post U.S. Apartment Rents Post Eighth Consecutive Month of Growth appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: U.S. apartment rents +0.03% MoM in July 2026; +1.0% YoY; eighth consecutive positive month

stories.summary: U.S. apartment rents rose just 0.03% month-over-month in July 2026 to an average of $1,747, marking the eighth consecutive month of positive growth but a notable deceleration. Year-over-year growth improved to 1.0%, but Apartments.com emphasized that elevated national supply levels are suppressing pricing power even as the market recovers from mid-2025 weakness.
stories.impact: Sustained supply pressure limits rent growth despite consistent positive momentum—a signal that new-supply deliveries continue to outpace demand absorption in major markets. Developers should expect compressed NOI growth and longer lease-up timelines even in growing metros. Cap rate expansion risk remains; refinancing windows for value-add deals are narrowing as rate relief stalls.

stories.title: Costa Mesa Multifamily Changes Hands for Value-Add Repositioning
stories.excerpt: Marcus & Millichap finalized the sale of 1990 Maple Ave., a 41-unit multifamily property in Costa Mesa. The property sold for $16.9 million or $412,195 per unit, approximately $550,000 above the property’s 2018 selling price. “Sundance West Apartment Homes presented a rare opportunity to acquire a low-density multifamily community in one of Orange County’s most supply-constrained rental markets,” said Matthew Kipp, senior managing director investments. “The property’s unique concentration of two- and three-bedroom floor plans and the meaningful capital improvements completed by prior ownership, including electrical upgrades and roof replacements, attracted significant investor interest. The competitive bidding environment allowed the seller to look beyond price alone and select a buyer whose local experience provided the highest confidence in execution.” Kipp and Tyler Leeson, executive managing director investments, in Marcus & Millichap’s Orange County office, marketed the property on behalf of the seller, a local family, exchanging out-of-state to reduce hands-on management, and procured the buyer, a professional investor acquiring for value-add repositioning. If you’re reading about the multifamily industry, you should be in the room with its leaders. Connect Apartments brings together the executives featured in Connect CRE’s coverage for an afternoon of high-level insights and unmatched networking on September 22 at The Biltmore in LA. The post Costa Mesa Multifamily Changes Hands for Value-Add Repositioning appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Costa Mesa 41-unit multifamily sold for $16.9M ($412K/unit); up $550K from 2018 price
Competitive bidding on low-density, supply-constrained Orange County rental asset
Two- and three-bedroom mix, deferred capital work (electrical, roof) attracted investors
stories.summary: Marcus & Millichap closed the sale of Sundance West Apartment Homes, a 41-unit multifamily property in Costa Mesa, for $16.9 million ($412,195 per unit), approximately $550,000 above its 2018 selling price. The property's unique two- and three-bedroom floor plan concentration and completed capital improvements (electrical upgrades, roof replacement) generated competitive bidding from professional investors. The seller, a local family, used the sale for a tax exchange.
stories.impact: Brisk bidding on small, well-maintained multifamily in Orange County confirms persistent supply scarcity in Southern California's coastal rental markets. Rising per-unit pricing reflects limited new construction—zoning/environmental constraints in OC limit new supply—sustaining rent growth and investor demand for value-add repositioning. Developers with entitlements for multifamily in supply-constrained OC submarkets have a 12–18 month window of strong acquisition appetite before broader rate-driven capital drying occurs.

stories.title: NYC Issues Partial Stop-Work Order at SL Green’s 750 Third Avenue Conversion
stories.excerpt: New York City’s Department of Buildings (DOB) has halted construction work at the third office-to-conversion project in Manhattan this month. The DOB issued a partial stop-work order at SL Green Realty’s $805 million conversion project at 750 Third Avenue in Midtown East, which is set to result in 680 residential units and potentially see 11 floors added. The halt comes after the near-collapse of the former Pfizer headquarters earlier in July, when steel beams at MetroLoft and David Werner’s 235 East 42nd Street project buckled and sparked the evacuation of 10 surrounding Midtown blocks. Earlier this week, GFP Real Estate’s conversion project at 222 Broadway in the Financial District was also halted after cracks were found on a newly added floor. In the case of 750 Third Avenue, it seems as if steel columns were not welded properly and inconsistencies were reported, according to the DOB. As a result, inspectors have temporarily stopped all steel work above the eighth floor at the 34-story property, according to The New York Times, which first reported the news. “During our structural reinforcement prep work, prior to beginning any overbuild work, we identified an on-site condition that differed from the plans that were submitted to the city, which was visible only after completing initial preparation work,” an SL Green spokesperson said in a statement to Commercial Observer. “There are no structural issues with the building, and we are already working with the licensed professional engineer of record to address this condition,” the spokesperson added. “We do not anticipate any impact to the overall project schedule, with other work ongoing, and have already submitted our request to rescind the partial stop work order.” While the Pfizer buckling certainly spurred a renewed scrutiny of ongoing conversion projects in New York City and an increased focus on safety, these types of partial stop-work orders are not uncommon. bullets: NYC DOB halts construction at SL Green's 750 Third Ave office-to-conversion ($805M project)
Defective steel welds above eighth floor; third Manhattan conversion stop-work in one month

stories.summary: New York City's Department of Buildings issued a partial stop-work order at SL Green Realty's $805 million office-to-residential conversion at 750 Third Avenue in Midtown East, halting all steel work above the eighth floor due to improperly welded steel columns and reported inconsistencies. This is the third Manhattan conversion project halted in one month—following the near-collapse at 235 East 42nd Street (MetroLoft/David Werner) and cracks at 222 Broadway (GFP Real Estate).
stories.impact: Cascading construction halts at major Manhattan conversions signal systemic quality-control and inspection failures, triggering regulatory tightening. This delays deliver of 680 units at 750 Third Ave and creates uncertainty on timeline/financing for large conversion projects citywide. Multifamily developers planning office conversions in NYC now face extended permitting timelines, higher inspection scrutiny, and potential cost overruns for structural remediation—reducing conversion project IRRs and shifting capital toward ground-up development in outer boroughs.

stories.title: New York Life Sees Leasing Momentum at 757 Third Ave. Amid Continued Renovations

New York Life is completing cosmetic lobby renovations and rolling out a prebuilt office program to drive leasing momentum.
stories.impact: Minimal direct multifamily impact; this is office leasing activity. However, sustained office occupancy at 757 Third Ave and comparable assets suggests that selective Midtown East office properties are stabilizing after years of hybrid-work pressure. This may reduce urgency for broad-based office-to-residential conversions in Midtown and preserve Class A office stock for office use, keeping conversion economics marginal and concentrating residential development in Hudson Yards, Long Island City, and outer boroughs.

stories.title: BGO, Yukon Real Estate Partners Sell 291K-SF Kansas Cold Storage Facility
stories.excerpt: BGO and Yukon Real Estate Partners announced the sale of New Century Cold Storage, a newly built 291,000-square-foot, plant-attached, rail-served cold storage warehouse in New Century, Kansas, to a MetLife Investment Management client. The facility, owned and co-developed through a joint venture between BGO and Yukon, was purpose-built as a plant-attached, build-to-suit warehouse for CJ Logistics America. “With its purpose-built design, strategic location, and direct integration with food production and logistics operations, we believe this facility will make a meaningful contribution to the strength and resilience of U.S. food supply chains for decades to come,” said Kevin Rivest, Managing Partner, BGO. The New Century facility is located within the Johnson County Airport Commission’s New Century AirCenter industrial park, with a direct rail spur to the building and access to the BNSF Railway transcontinental intermodal facility. The property is positioned less than four miles from Interstate 35. The post BGO, Yukon Real Estate Partners Sell 291K-SF Kansas Cold Storage Facility appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: BGO and Yukon sell New Century Cold Storage facility in Kansas to MetLife Investment client
291,000-SF plant-attached, rail-served build-to-suit warehouse in Johnson County AirCenter

stories.summary: BGO and Yukon Real Estate Partners sold New Century Cold Storage, a newly built 291,000-square-foot plant-attached, rail-served cold storage facility in New Century, Kansas, to a MetLife Investment Management client. The facility was purpose-built as a build-to-suit warehouse for CJ Logistics America within the Johnson County Airport Commission's industrial park.
stories.impact: No direct multifamily relevance; this is a logistics/industrial asset sale. Industrial capital flow to Kansas may indicate broader capital deployment in Midwest secondary markets, potentially signaling supply-chain regionalization that could eventually boost employment and indirectly support multifamily demand in Kansas City metro, but this effect is distant.

stories.title: AI Platform Clay Leases 44K SF with Swig Company
stories.excerpt: The Swig Company has leased 44,000 square feet at The Mills Building to artificial intelligence platform Clay. The lease was announced two weeks after Swig refinanced the circa-1891 property at 220 Montgomery St. in San Francisco’s Financial District. “The Mills Building continues to attract companies seeking a workplace that reflects their culture and ambitions,” said Stacia Keisner, SVP of asset management at The Swig Company. “Clay’s lease is another example of an innovative business choosing downtown San Francisco to recruit talent, foster collaboration, and position themselves for long-term success.” Cory Kristoff, EVP, director of leasing, added, “Through our focused spec suite initiative at the Mills Building, we have leased more than 102,000 square feet of space year to date, representing approximately 21% of the property. We are encouraged by this strong leasing momentum and expect it to continue throughout the remainder of the year and beyond.” Bart O’Connor, Mark Geisreiter and Hannah Potter of Newmark represented The Swig Company. Maurice (Mo) Spikes, Derek Feinman and Aaron Ellison of Newmark represented Clay. The post AI Platform Clay Leases 44K SF with Swig Company appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: AI platform Clay leases 44,000 SF at Mills Building, San Francisco Financial District
Swig Company has leased 102,000 SF YTD (21% of property) via spec-suite strategy
Lease follows property refinance; downtown SF office leasing gains momentum
stories.summary: Artificial intelligence platform Clay signed a 44,000-square-foot lease at The Mills Building (circa-1891, 220 Montgomery Street) in San Francisco's Financial District, operated by The Swig Company. This lease is part of Swig's strong 2026 leasing momentum: 102,000 square feet leased year-to-date (21% of the property) through a focused spec-suite initiative. The lease came two weeks after Swig refinanced the property.
stories.impact: SF Financial District office leasing—especially tech/AI tenants—signals downtown revitalization that may arrest residential demand softness. However, office-to-residential conversion economics in SOMA/FiDi remain challenged by elevated construction costs and modest rent growth. Multifamily developers should monitor: if office leasing sustains, conversion projects lose urgency; if it falters, regulatory/construction delays (per article 6) make conversions economically unfeasible, concentrating new supply in outer neighborhoods (Mission, NOPA, Sunset).

stories.title: NYC Selects Slate Property Group, Hudson Companies to Build 980 Homes in LIC
stories.excerpt: A development team made up of Slate Property Group, Hudson Companies and Volunteers of America-Greater New York has been chosen to create nearly 1,000 new homes upon a vacant parcel in Long Island City, Queens. The 70,000-square-foot development, at 54-42 Second Street, will be called the Orion, and two-thirds of its units will be set aside as affordable housing. “It is exactly what New York needs,” David Schwartz, principal and co-founder of Slate Property Group, said in a statement. “And we look forward to working with City Hall to get shovels in the ground as soon as possible.” The parcel sits within the 30-acre Hunter’s Point South housing complex. When completed, Hunter’s Point South is expected to feature approximately 5,000 new homes, roughly 3,000 of which will be affordable. The city’s Department of Housing Preservation and Development (HPD) began courting developers for the site, known as Parcel E, in June of last year. The request for proposals came with the requirement that Parcel E host more affordable homes than previous phases. The Orion will include approximately 980 new apartments. Two-thirds of the apartments, roughly 658 units, will be income-restricted, affordable to extremely low- to moderate-income households. Approximately 150 units will be set aside as supportive apartments. “Reaching households at every income level in a high-opportunity neighborhood like Hunter’s Point reflects a simple belief: Where New Yorkers live shouldn’t come down to income alone,” said Laszlo Syrop, principal and head of acquisitions at Hudson Companies. The mixed-use community, designed by Marvel Architects, will feature an affordable child care center, a workforce development center and a community pool. Approximately 6,000 square feet of ground-floor commercial retail space will also be made available along Second Street and Center Boulevard. bullets: NYC selects Slate Property Group, Hudson Companies for 980-unit LIC development (Parcel E)
70,000-SF site at 54-42 Second Street; 66% of units set aside as affordable

stories.summary: NYC's Department of Housing Preservation and Development selected a development team led by Slate Property Group and Hudson Companies to build 'The Orion,' a nearly 1,000-unit residential project at 54-42 Second Street in Long Island City, Queens. The 70,000-square-foot site will include approximately 650 affordable units (two-thirds of total units). The parcel sits within the 30-acre Hunter's Point South complex, which is expected to deliver roughly 5,000 total homes (approximately 3,000 affordable) when fully built out.
stories.impact: Major public-private residential pipeline in LIC confirms sustained multifamily demand in Queens but signals regulatory preference for dense, affordability-heavy development. This constrains for-profit developer margins in LIC and shifts capital toward outer-borough ground-up projects with lower land costs and reduced affordability requirements. Developers targeting Queens should expect persistent public land disposition and affordability mandates; conventional value-add acquisition/repositioning will face competition from subsidized public projects, compressing cap rates.
